strengths: Addresses timely and practically important problem of protecting images from diffusion-based editing attacks
Novel optimization-free training paradigm enables dramatic efficiency improvements (250,000x speedup from days to milliseconds), enabling real-world deployment
Comprehensive evaluation with multiple perceptual metrics (SSIM, PSNR, FSIM, CLIP-T), ablation studies, robustness analysis, and extension to video content
Strong quantitative results across unseen test data demonstrating good generalization and robustness against counter-attacks (JPEG compression, denoising)
First work extending image immunization to video content with demonstrated effectiveness
Well-presented with clear methodology, reproducible implementation details, and code availability
weaknesses: Limited architectural and algorithmic novelty—while optimization-free training is novel, core components (UNet++, diffusion inpainting) are standard; contribution is primarily in training strategy
Narrow evaluation scope: heavily focuses on SDEdit; limited quantitative comparison with other diffusion-based editing tools; only 2 main baselines in quantitative tables
Small training dataset (1,000 images) and limited unseen test set (20% of data); video evaluation extremely limited (4 videos, 64 frames each)
Missing theoretical justification for loss design choices; lacks analysis of when/why the formulation works or failure case discussion
No statistical significance testing, error bars, or confidence intervals; unclear if differences between methods are statistically significant
Prompt dependency not fully addressed; while ChatGPT generates diverse prompts, risk of prompt shift remains; prompt-agnostic experiments limited
No human perceptual studies validating imperceptibility claims; relies on proxy metrics (SSIM, PSNR) which may not fully capture perceptual quality
Limited analysis of scalability (high-resolution images), hyperparameter sensitivity beyond α, and GPU memory requirements; training time still significant (~22 hours)

strengths: Significant practical speedup (~250,000x vs. PhotoGuard) achieved through optimization-free inference—genuinely useful for real-world deployment
Comprehensive experimental scope including image and video experiments, ablation studies, and non-human object generalization
Well-organized presentation with clear methodology (Algorithm 1) and intuitive two-stage training framework
Provides code and project webpage, supporting reproducibility
Addresses timely problem of protecting images against emerging diffusion-based editing attacks
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: core contribution is straightforward application of adversarial perturbations with pre-trained models; the 'optimization-free' framing is primarily an engineering choice rather than fundamental innovation

Incomplete robustness evaluation: only tests JPEG compression and basic denoising; lacks evaluation against other perturbation removal techniques, resizing, format conversion, or adversarial attacks specifically designed to break the immunization

Weak generalization claims: evaluation uses same-dataset 80/20 split with no true out-of-distribution testing; training data is limited to 1,000 images; method trained exclusively on inpainting-based diffusion editing

Problematic evaluation metrics: relies on SSIM/PSNR (known to correlate poorly with perceptual quality); CLIP-T is text-image similarity metric, not designed for imperceptibility; Figure 11 shows visible artifacts contradicting imperceptibility claims; user study only tests intuitiveness not robustness

Insufficient baseline comparisons: only compares against PhotoGuard variants and weak Random Noise; missing comparisons with alternative defense mechanisms, watermarking, or concurrent robustness work; some comparisons unfairly specified
Critical hyperparameter (loss weight α) inadequately justified: selected based on only 100 images with no sensitivity analysis or guidelines for new applications
Video results underdeveloped: only 4 videos tested with no quantitative metrics analogous to image evaluation
Loss weight selection and other design choices (UNet++ architecture, SAM segmentation) lack proper justification or ablation studies

strengths: Novel optimization-free approach achieving 250,000× speedup over prior work (milliseconds vs. hours per image), enabling practical large-scale deployment
Comprehensive experimental evaluation including robustness against counter-attacks, ablation studies, human study with 67 participants, and evaluation on both seen and unseen data
First extension of image immunization to video content with demonstrated temporal consistency
Addresses timely and important problem of protecting images/videos from diffusion-based malicious editing
Excellent clarity and presentation with well-motivated methodology, clear algorithm descriptions, and comprehensive visualizations
Demonstrates generalization beyond human-centric data to non-human objects (animals) without retraining
Strong empirical results consistently outperforming baselines (PhotoGuard, Random Noise) across multiple metrics while maintaining imperceptibility
Technically sound approach with well-motivated two-stage framework and appropriate loss functions for both imperceptibility and editing disruption
weaknesses: Limited architectural novelty—individual components (UNet++, SAM, Stable Diffusion) are existing; primary contribution is training strategy rather than technical innovation
Relatively narrow evaluation scope—primarily tested against Stable Diffusion inpainting and InstructPix2Pix; unclear generalization to other editing paradigms or future models
Small dataset scale and limited diversity—only 1,000 images from CCP dataset; video evaluation on just 4 videos; no evaluation on major benchmarks (COCO, ImageNet)
Loss function specifically tuned to Stable Diffusion inpainting; training on single editing model type may not transfer to fundamentally different approaches
Generalization concerns partially contradicted by prompt-agnostic claims—performance varies across different prompts (Figure 6 shows this variation)
Limited theoretical analysis—no principled framework or theoretical guarantees explaining why training strategy is optimal
Incomplete analysis of failure cases and adversarial scenarios; unclear characterization of method limitations
Training computational costs not discussed—only inference cost reported; no details on training time or GPU requirements
Video evaluation is preliminary—temporal consistency not explicitly evaluated; no comparison with other potential video protection methods
